query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A minor addition of an interfacial‐active dopant that segregates to the lamellar colony boundaries will enhance boundary cohesion and reduce microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation, thereby improving both strength and ductility relative to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloys with dual-phase lamellar colonies that exhibit brittleness and limited ductility at room temperature due to microcrack initiation at internal boundaries.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor concentration of an interfacial‐active dopant during alloy processing to promote its segregation to the colony boundaries.
generation.conditions: Processing conditions that favor the formation of lamellar colonies and allow effective dopant segregation, followed by room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced interphase cohesion at the lamellar colony boundaries due to dopant segregation.
generation.mechanism: The dopant segregates to the internal boundaries, lowering the local boundary energy and stress concentrations. This mitigates microcrack initiation and propagation during tensile loading, leading to simultaneous improvements in strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified baseline, the doped alloy will exhibit improved tensile strength and greater ductility, with a reduction in microcrack formation at the colony boundaries.
generation.baseline: An unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies that is prone to boundary-induced microcracking and limited ductility.
generation.boundary: The intervention is effective only when the dopant is added in a minor, carefully controlled amount that promotes segregation without forming deleterious secondary phases, and within processing conditions that preserve the lamellar structure.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal dopant concentration and processing parameters for achieving the desired segregation and mechanical property improvements remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples under identical conditions: one as an unmodified control and one with the minor dopant addition. Confirm dopant segregation to the colony boundaries using microscopic and spectroscopic analyses, then perform room-temperature tensile tests on both sets.
measurements: Microscopic analysis of dopant distribution and microcrack initiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the control, or if dopant segregation without undesirable phase formation is not confirmed, the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount of interfacial-active dopant (e.g., ~0.5 at.% Nb) into the eutectic high-entropy alloy will lead to segregation at the lamellar colony boundaries, which improves interfacial cohesion and reduces microcrack initiation, thereby enhancing both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility.
drafts.material_initial_state: A conventional eutectic high-entropy alloy composed of dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries prone to microcracking during tensile deformation at room temperature.
drafts.intervention: Add a minor concentration of an interfacial-active element (e.g., approximately 0.5 at.% niobium) to the alloy composition during processing.
drafts.conditions: Maintain conventional casting and controlled cooling protocols to ensure lamellar colony formation while allowing the dopant to preferentially segregate to internal boundaries without forming secondary brittle phases.
drafts.structural_mediator: Modified interphase boundaries enriched with the dopant which result in lower local stress concentrations and greater resistance to crack initiation.
drafts.mechanism: The Nb dopant is expected to segregate to the internal boundaries, reducing the boundary energy and enhancing interface cohesion. This change blunts crack tip propagation while also refining lamellar spacing, which together impede dislocation motion and delay crack initiation, yielding a material that is both stronger and more ductile under tensile loads.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, the doped alloy should exhibit a statistically significant increase in yield strength accompanied by improved tensile ductility at room temperature.
drafts.baseline: The undoped eutectic high-entropy alloy shows high strength but limited ductility due to microcrack initiation at numerous internal boundaries.
drafts.boundary: The success of this intervention relies on ensuring that the dopant segregates exclusively to the boundaries without leading to the formation of brittle intermetallic phases. The beneficial effect is anticipated only within a narrow dopant concentration window (around 0.5 at.%); higher concentrations may trigger unfavorable phase formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of eutectic HEA samples with 0, 0.5, and 1.0 at.% Nb added under identical processing conditions. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) combined with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) to verify dopant segregation at the internal boundaries. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests on each sample and perform fractography to identify crack initiation sites.
measurements: TEM and EDS of lamellar boundaries to confirm Nb segregation
Room-temperature tensile stress-strain curves to measure yield strength and ductility
Fractographic analysis to determine the presence and initiation of microcracking
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-doped samples do not display a statistically significant increase in both yield strength and tensile ductility compared to the undoped sample, or if brittle phases/intermetallics are observed disrupting the lamellar structure, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Minor boron additions to eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) will reduce boundary-related microcracking by enhancing interphase cohesion, thereby improving both strength and ductility at room temperature compared to the undoped lamellar-colony baseline.
drafts.material_initial_state: An as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies prone to microcracking under tensile load at room temperature.
drafts.intervention: Introduce a small concentration of boron (e.g., 0.1–0.3 at.%) into the melt prior to casting to promote boundary cohesion and mitigate crack nucleation within the lamellar colonies.
drafts.conditions: Vacuum induction melting, followed by casting and a short homogenization (e.g., at ~1000 °C), then cooling to room temperature in air to retain boron at interphase boundaries.
drafts.structural_mediator: Boron segregation at lamellar phase boundaries, contributing to reduced interfacial energy and increased local cohesion.
drafts.mechanism: By segregating to interphase boundaries, boron lowers boundary energy and promotes stronger bonding between phases, reducing the propensity for microcrack initiation and propagation during tensile loading at room temperature.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped baseline, the boron-doped EHEA will show a measurable increase (on the order of at least 20%) in yield strength due to enhanced boundary strength, and an increase (on the order of 30–50%) in total elongation, reflecting improved ductility and delayed fracture.
drafts.baseline: The baseline is the same EHEA composition without boron addition, which forms relatively brittle lamellar colonies that tend to fail prematurely under tension due to inter-lamellar microcracking.
drafts.boundary: Excess boron (>0.3 at.%) may lead to detrimental boride precipitates that embrittle the microstructure, offsetting the beneficial effects of boundary strengthening. The efficacy also depends on the specific composition and processing route used.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two identical EHEA melts: one reference batch without boron and one with a small (0.2 at.%) boron addition. Cast both into identical molds and homogenize at ~1000 °C before air-cooling. Machine standard tensile specimens from each batch for room-temperature testing.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
Fracture surface characterization (SEM or TEM of lamellar boundaries)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not consistently exhibit higher yield strength and greater tensile elongation than the undoped baseline, or if fracture surfaces do not show evidence of reduced microcrack formation at lamellar boundaries, the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing nanoscale precipitates at colony boundaries in eutectic high-entropy alloys will improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility by mitigating microcrack initiation and propagation while enhancing load transfer across boundaries.
drafts.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies and numerous internal boundaries.
drafts.intervention: Incorporation of nanoscale precipitates at colony boundaries via controlled thermal treatment and alloying additions.
drafts.mechanism: The nanoscale precipitates will act as crack-arresting sites, reducing the likelihood of microcrack propagation. Additionally, they will enhance load transfer across colony boundaries, improving strength and ductility simultaneously.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, the modified alloy will exhibit increased tensile strength and ductility at room temperature, with reduced brittleness.
drafts.baseline: Unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies exhibiting room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility.
drafts.boundary: Effectiveness of the intervention may depend on the size, distribution, and composition of the nanoscale precipitates, as well as the specific alloy system and processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples: one with nanoscale precipitates introduced at colony boundaries via controlled thermal treatment and alloying additions, and one unmodified baseline. Perform room-temperature tensile tests on both sets.
measurements: Fracture surface analysis to assess microcrack initiation and propagation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy does not show simultaneous improvement in tensile strength and ductility compared to the baseline, or if microcrack initiation and propagation are not reduced, the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled amount of ductile phase reinforcement within the lamellar colonies of eutectic high-entropy alloys will enhance both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility.
drafts.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloys with dual-phase lamellar colonies exhibiting brittleness and limited ductility.
drafts.intervention: Incorporation of a ductile phase (e.g., a softer metal or alloy) into the lamellar structure.
drafts.conditions: The intervention should be applied during the alloy processing stage, ensuring uniform distribution of the ductile phase within the lamellar colonies.
drafts.structural_mediator: The presence of the ductile phase will create a more favorable stress distribution and energy absorption mechanism during deformation.
drafts.mechanism: The ductile phase will absorb stress and deform plastically, reducing the likelihood of microcracking in the brittle lamellar structure during tensile loading.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The modified eutectic high-entropy alloy will exhibit increased tensile strength and improved ductility compared to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.
drafts.baseline: Unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloys with dual-phase lamellar colonies showing limited ductility and brittleness.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is limited to eutectic high-entropy alloys with specific lamellar structures and may not apply to other alloy systems or processing methods.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct tensile tests on both modified and unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloys to compare strength and ductility.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy does not show a statistically significant increase in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the unmodified alloy, the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introduction of a controlled amount of lattice distortion through targeted alloying can improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
drafts.material_initial_state: Dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries in eutectic high-entropy alloys
drafts.intervention: Targeted alloying to introduce controlled lattice distortion
drafts.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion and its effect on dislocation movement and grain boundary stability
drafts.mechanism: The introduction of controlled lattice distortion can hinder dislocation movement, thereby increasing strength, while also enhancing grain boundary stability, which can improve ductility by reducing the initiation and propagation of microcracks.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Improved strength and room-temperature tensile ductility compared to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline
drafts.boundary: The optimal amount of lattice distortion and the specific alloying elements used

falsification_experiment.design: Tensile testing of specimens with varying levels of targeted alloying under room-temperature conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduction of controlled lattice distortion through targeted alloying does not result in improved strength and room-temperature tensile ductility compared to the unmodified baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.
